overview.title: nobg.
paragraphs: nobg is a terminal tool that removes image backgrounds. It is written in PyTorch, using a custom model inspired by SegFormer, an architecture for image segmentation.

pipeline.title: From image to transparent PNG
pipeline.intro: The command-line tool runs one image through the network, builds a foreground mask, and writes a PNG with transparency.

steps.title: Image
steps.description: Read the image from disk. Keep its original dimensions for the final PNG.

steps.title: Preprocessing
steps.description: Resize to the model input size and normalize pixel values so the network receives consistent inputs.

steps.title: Encoder
steps.description: Extract visual features at four scales. A feature is a learned number that helps describe an area of the image.

steps.title: Decoder
steps.description: Combine the four scales to predict one foreground score for each position in a low-resolution grid.

steps.title: Optional refiner
steps.description: Use the image and early features to correct the decoder prediction. It is designed to improve local detail, especially around edges.

steps.title: Mask
steps.description: Sigmoid converts scores to values from 0 to 1. The CLI uses a 0.5 threshold by default, or keeps soft values with --alpha.

steps.title: Transparent PNG
steps.description: Resize the mask to the original image dimensions. Save it as the PNG alpha channel, which controls transparency.

architecture.title: Model architecture
architecture.intro: The model has three main parts, a four stage encoder, one decoder, and a mask refiner

diagram.caption: Solid arrows show the main path. Dashed arrows show extra inputs to the refiner and the path used when refinement is disabled.

labels.encoder: MiT encoder · overlapping patches, reduced attention, MixFFN

explanations.title: MiT encoder
explanations.description: The image passes through four stages, each at a smaller resolution. The first stages keep more spatial detail; the later ones capture larger shapes. The stages output 32, 64, 160, and 256 channels.

explanations.title: Transformer blocks
explanations.description: Each stage starts with overlapping image patches. Attention helps different parts of the image share information, while spatial reduction keeps the work manageable. MixFFN also mixes information from nearby positions.

explanations.title: Decoder
explanations.description: The decoder takes the four feature maps, resizes them to the same grid, and combines them. From that, it makes the first foreground prediction.

explanations.title: Optional refiner
explanations.description: The first prediction may lose detail around edges. The refiner looks at the image, the first encoder feature map, and the decoder prediction to learn a correction. That correction is added before sigmoid produces the mask.

details.title: Tensor shapes at a 256 × 256 input
paragraphs: A tensor is a multi-dimensional array. B is the number of images in a batch. C is the number of channels; H and W are height and width.
These dimensions describe the default encoder and binary decoder.

rows.label: Decoder projections
rows.value: Four maps, each B × 256 × 64 × 64 after resizing

rows.label: Final prediction
rows.value: B × 1 × 256 × 256 with the refiner, or after standard upsampling

details.title: Inside a MiT stage
paragraphs: Each stage begins with an overlapping convolutional patch embedding and contains two transformer blocks in the default model. Within each block, attention and MixFFN each have a skip connection.
For attention, queries come from the full grid. Keys and values can come from a smaller grid. This reduces memory and computation.

rows.label: Patch embedding
rows.value: First stage: 7 × 7 kernel, stride 4. Later stages: 3 × 3 kernel, stride 2.

rows.label: MixFFN
rows.value: Linear layer, 3 × 3 depthwise convolution, GELU, then linear layer

details.title: Decoder and refiner blocks
paragraphs: The decoder projects each scale to 256 channels, resizes to the 64 × 64 grid, concatenates, and fuses with a 1 × 1 convolution. A final 1 × 1 convolution produces the foreground score, also called a logit.

The refiner uses three resolutions: quarter, half, and full input size. Its convolution blocks use GroupNorm and SiLU. The last correction layer starts at zero, so refinement initially leaves the decoder output unchanged.

rows.label: Decoder output
rows.value: A single logit for each foreground location

rows.label: Refiner inputs
rows.value: Stage 1 features, raw decoder logits, and the RGB image

rows.label: Residual result
rows.value: Upsampled decoder logits + learned one-channel correction

rows.label: Probability
rows.value: Sigmoid maps each final logit to a value between 0 and 1

training.title: Training
training.intro: During training, the model sees an image and a reference mask. It predicts its own mask, measures the difference, and updates the parameters that are allowed to learn.
datasetParagraphs: DUTS is a dataset of photographs paired with masks that mark the main visible object. The current training paths use DUTS-TR, its training set.
Augmentation makes changed versions of training images, such as flips, rotations, crops, and brightness changes. The matching masks receive the same geometric changes.

Validation checks the model on a held-out 10% split of DUTS-TR without random training augmentations. A checkpoint saves model and training state after each epoch. Visual samples compare images, reference masks, and predictions.

lossExplanations.title: Dice loss
lossExplanations.description: Measures region overlap between the predicted foreground and the reference foreground. More overlap means lower loss.

lossExplanations.title: BCE
lossExplanations.description: Binary cross-entropy measures pixel-level prediction error. It penalizes confident wrong foreground or background predictions.
